items.why: It cleanly distinguishes the Levite’s stated purpose from Micah’s house, which he reaches only en route.
The answer is found by adjacency, and calling the conditional blessing a “request” is somewhat unnatural.
Resolving the quoted “you” correctly identifies Micah’s mother rather than Micah as the curse speaker.
The final since-clause states the reason verbatim, though it does distinguish priestly status from birthplace.
It strongly distinguishes the relatives Abimelek addresses as intermediaries from the citizens receiving his message.
It distinguishes the reported departure into the fields that triggers the ambush from Abimelek’s later sighting.
The sender is explicit, but the nearby conflict between Zebul and Gaal gives the role distinction some value.
It distinguishes Abimelek’s immediate purpose of setting the tower alight from his broader attack on it.
“Does something” is too vague and forces the reader to decode an abstract reference rather than a clear event.
The reason is stated directly, while the trees’ subsequent approach to the fig tree is not a plausible cause.
It tests Zebul’s reinterpretation of the apparent people as mountain shadows.
It sharply distinguishes whom the mother says will make the image from the silversmith who later actually makes it.
The fire is the explicit cause of death, whereas entering the stronghold is merely an earlier action.
The reason is explicit and closely duplicates the olive-tree pattern, with an implausible subsequent-event rival.
It cleanly separates the priesthood lasting until captivity from the idol’s use while God’s house was at Shiloh.
The curse appears to describe the punishment itself, so asking what happens “after” the punishment is misleading.
The passage directly attributes Jotham’s relocation to fear of Abimelek, making the contrast clear but easy.
The cumbersome reference to “the residence the Danites visit” makes a simple route-sequence question unnatural.
The final sentence explicitly names Abimelek as dead, bypassing the pronoun-role interpretation in the killing.
It strongly distinguishes the five men’s initial seizure from the priest’s later handling of the same objects.
It distinguishes the immediate prompt—the men’s shouting—from their earlier act of overtaking the Danites.
The reader must resolve “him” to Jerub-Baal despite Abimelek’s nearby mention.
The passage explicitly links prosperity to the land’s abundance, not to the comparison with the Sidonians.
It distinguishes the people’s isolation as the reason no rescue comes from the attack that creates the need.
It cleanly separates the priest they ask from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
It contrasts the five spies who enter and take the objects with the priest and soldiers remaining at the gate.
The purpose clause gives God’s listening as the intended result, distinct from the ensuing fable about kingship.
It requires resolving “it” to the land rather than confusing the object of takeover with the people living there.
It distinguishes the explicit cause—lack of an inheritance—from the nearby background statement that Israel had no king.
The thornbush is plainly invited to rule the trees, while gods and humans are mentioned only as enjoying wine.
It clearly distinguishes cursing during the festival meal from the earlier grape gathering and treading.
